column4: The section’s dictionary form قِوَام (what a thing stands by) names support; 4:5 calls property قِيَامًا لَكُمْ, a support for people’s lives, giving that secondary root sense a direct Quranic use.
The section’s q-w-m root links standing and rising; here the heavens and earth stand by God’s command, then people emerge from the earth when called, joining support with resurrection.
The section’s dictionary note defines support as what prevents a thing from falling; 35:41 says God holds the heavens and earth lest they cease, an explicit cosmic instance of that sustaining role.
The section names the support that keeps a thing from falling; this verse says God holds the sky lest it fall upon the earth, making the image of a sustaining hand concrete.
The section’s upright human is returned downward; Moses’ words give the full earth-cycle: God creates people from earth, returns them to it, then brings them out again.
The section connects the body’s return with the ground; this verse says God caused people to grow from the earth like plants, giving the return-to-earth image a creation-side counterpart.
The section’s downward return is one phase of a larger cycle; this verse says God will return people to earth and bring them forth again.
The section moves from a formed human to a lowered one; this verse traces the body from dust through womb and infant stages to maturity and frail old age, and pairs that with dead earth revived.
The section’s return to earth leads to a later rising; this next verse says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves, completing the resurrection scene beside 22:5.
The section’s upright body has a downward arc; this verse explicitly moves human life from weakness to strength and back to weakness and old age.
The section describes a human made in the best upright form; this verse names the human’s weakness, a bodily limit beside that well-formed beginning.
The section’s fall can be heard as bodily decline; this verse says a person given long life is reversed in creation until strength and knowledge recede.
The section’s upright body can descend into frailty; this verse says some are returned to decrepit age, knowing little after having known much.
The section’s body moves from creation toward decline; this verse traces people from dust and a drop through childhood and maturity to old age and death.
The section describes a human created in a fitted form; this neighboring passage asks from what a person was created, introducing its bodily sequence.
The section’s تقويم is the human made upright and well-proportioned; this verse says God created and proportioned the person, a direct parallel in a passage about life’s stages.
The section’s body returns downward; this verse says God causes the person to die and be buried, giving the descent a literal bodily endpoint.
The section’s descent is not the end of the human course; this verse says God will raise the person again, continuing the death and burial of 80:21.
The section’s 95:4 speaks of creating and proportioning the human; this verse says God created, fashioned, and balanced the person, a direct account of bodily form.
The section’s image concerns a body given its form; this next verse says God composed the human in whatever form He willed, completing the bodily shaping in 82:7.
The section’s 95:7 asks what makes a person deny judgment after being created; this next verse says, “Rather, you deny the Recompense,” following the formation in 82:7 and 82:8.
The section’s human stands in the best form; this verse says God fashioned people and made their forms good, alongside making earth a settled place.
The section’s body is made in a fitting form; this verse says God created and shaped people and made their forms good.
The section’s root note describes تقويم as setting something upright and removing its crookedness; this verse says God created and proportioned, a direct lexical and bodily parallel.
The section’s image is of a body given its measure; this next verse says God determined and guided after creating and proportioning in 87:2.
The section depicts a body brought to its completed standing form; this verse pairs creating and fashioning humanity with the command to the angels to prostrate to Adam.
The section describes the human as fashioned in a fitting form; this verse says God fashioned Adam and breathed into him of His spirit, followed by the command to prostrate.
The section’s upright human recalls the completed formation of Adam; this verse says God fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit, then commands the angels to prostrate.
The section asks what follows the human’s finely fashioned body; the garden owner’s companion says God created him from dust, then a drop, then fashioned him as a man, and challenges his denial.
The section’s 95:7 questions denial of judgment; this neighboring verse states the garden owner’s denial of the Hour, while 18:37 answers with the human’s creation from dust and a drop.
The section starts from the completed human form; this verse gives its bodily beginning as an extract of clay, setting the human body within a creation sequence.
The section’s upright body begins in a lowly origin; this verse says the human seed is placed in a secure lodging, between the clay origin in 23:12 and bodily formation in 23:14.
The section describes a body brought to its finest form; this verse traces its formation through a clot, lump, bones, and flesh before calling it another creation.
The section’s human is finely formed; this verse says God perfected what He created and began the human’s creation from clay.
The section’s formed body has an earthly beginning; this verse says humanity’s descendants come from an extract of a despised fluid, continuing the creation sequence.
The section’s image is the completed human body; this verse says God fashioned the human and breathed into him of His spirit, then gave hearing, sight, and hearts.
The section describes a human brought to a fitting form; this verse says God shapes people in their mothers’ wombs as He wills.
The section speaks of a human formed in the best proportion; this verse swears by the soul and the One who proportioned it, beginning a passage about the soul’s two directions.
The section’s أَسْفَلَ سَافِلِينَ places a human at the lowest depth; this verse uses the same root in الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ for hypocrites’ lowest level in the Fire.
The section sends a human down to the lowest; this verse calls the abyss his “mother” when his scales are light, a concrete image of a low final destination.
The section connects bodily descent to 7:176, where a man inclines to earth; this preceding verse introduces him as one who sheds the signs he had been given.
The section itself names this scene: a man who could have been raised by the signs instead clings to earth (أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ), a direct reversal of elevation and descent.
The section links 7:176’s earth-bound man with denial; this next verse calls the example of those who deny God’s signs and wrong themselves an evil one, completing that warning.
The section describes height that depends on support; this verse pictures a good word as a tree with a firm root and branches reaching high, a clear image of rooted support and elevation.
The section asks what keeps a human standing; this next verse says God makes believers firm with a firm word in worldly life and the Hereafter, continuing the tree parable’s concern with stability.
The section notes that مَمْنُون means cut off and names مَنّة as sustaining strength; this verse promises believers who do good an أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, an uncut reward.
The section reads مَمْنُون as “cut off”; this verse gives believers who do good an أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, directly echoing the unbroken reward promised in 95:6.

The section recalls standing before God on the Day of Resurrection; this preceding verse asks whether those who cheat in measure expect to be raised. The next verse calls it a great day, and 83:6 says people stand before the Lord.
The section’s bodily standing recalls judgment; this verse calls the resurrection day a great day, and the next verse, 83:6, says people stand before the Lord of the worlds.
The section’s q-w-m root names standing and resurrection; this verse says people stand before the Lord of the worlds on the day that judges those who cheated in measure.
The section’s 95:5 and 95:6 divide people by their end; this continuation of 83:6 says the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, introducing their fate after the standing for judgment.

The section’s 95:7 asks what can make a person deny judgment; this verse directly answers deniers who claim they will not be raised after death, saying they will be raised and informed of their deeds.
The section moves from human creation to return; this verse asks how people can disbelieve in God after death, life, death again, and return to Him.

The section connects al-balad with bodies returned to earth; this verse opens at a town fallen upon its roofs, then recounts God reviving a dead man and his mount, joining a ruined place with bodily return to life.
The section’s body is formed and then sent downward; this verse says God begins creation, repeats it, and to Him people return.
The section’s return to earth leads to another emergence; this verse asks whether people see that God begins creation and then repeats it.
The section puts human creation and return on an earthly ground; this verse tells people to travel the earth, see how creation began, and recognize the later creation.
The section asks what becomes of the body lowered to earth; these deniers ask whether they will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones.
The section’s image concerns the body’s return and reappearance; this next verse extends the deniers’ question to their forefathers, completing the challenge in 56:47.
The section places death within a return to God; this verse commands the answer that the former and later generations will all be gathered.
The section’s descent does not end in disappearance; this next verse says the gathered generations meet at an appointed time, completing 56:49.
The section’s 95:5, 95:6, and 95:7 turn from bodily form to judgment; this verse voices the same objection about whether bones and fragments can be raised as a new creation.
The section moves from a formed body to its return; this verse voices the objection that decomposed bones cannot be brought back to life.
The section’s body is returned and raised; this answer says the One who made it the first time will give life to the bones, completing 36:78.
The section asks what follows the body’s lowering; this verse presents the denier’s doubt that God can gather his bones.
The section’s body is formed with a particular stature; this answer says God can restore even the fingertips, completing the challenge about reassembling bones.
The section describes a human body fashioned and held upright; this verse says God created people and strengthened their frames, and can replace them with others like them.
The section returns the human to earth; this verse records deniers asking whether they will be recreated after death and becoming dust.
The section’s earthly return is not the final state; this next verse says God knows what the earth diminishes of them and keeps a record.
The section joins the first human creation to the final return; this verse rejects the idea that God was unable to create first and says people doubt the new creation.
The section returns the human body to the lowest; this verse says the disbeliever, seeing his deeds on the warned-of Day, will wish he were dust.
The section’s final question challenges denial of judgment; this verse gives the claim that life ends with death and time alone, the denial to which 45:26 replies.
The section’s body returns and is raised; this next verse says deniers demand their forefathers be brought back, completing the challenge in 45:24.
The section asks what makes people deny judgment after creation; this next verse answers that God gives life and death and will gather people on the Day of Resurrection.
The section’s created body is lowered to earth; these deniers ask whether they will rise after dying, becoming dust and bones.
The section’s 95:7 asks why people deny the recompense; this next verse says the deniers call the promise of resurrection a tale of the ancients.
The section sets the upright body against a downward fate; this verse contrasts one walking fallen on his face with one walking upright on a straight path, making bodily posture a figure of guidance.
The section’s high-to-low movement has an explicit counterpart in this verse: the Event lowers some and raises others, describing a reversal of rank.
The section’s descent follows a moral distinction; this passage begins with the one who transgresses, whose outcome is spelled out in the next verses.
The section’s low outcome can follow a person’s choice; this next verse says the transgressor preferred the nearer life, completing the description begun in 79:37.
The section’s q-w-m root names standing before God; this verse describes one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains the self, giving the upright stance a judgment context.
The section swears by “this secure city”; Abraham asks God to make “this city” safe and provide its people, giving a prayer counterpart to the same البلد.
The section names “this secure city”; Abraham’s prayer uses البلد and asks that it be safe, matching the city’s particular scene.
Like 95:3, this oath names “this city”; the same surah later says in 90:4 that God created the human in hardship, placing the human image under the city’s setting.
The section names the secure city; this verse calls it البلدة whose Lord is to be worshipped and says He made it sacred, identifying the same kind of place.
The section moves from a made body to its final division; this verse shows one group’s faces bright on that Day, beginning the bodily contrast completed by the dusty faces in 80:40 and 80:41.
The section’s low outcome is bodily; this verse shows other faces covered with dust, the opposite appearance to 80:38 and the beginning of their fate in 80:41 and 80:42.
The section’s lowest outcome is separated from the exception for faith and good deeds; this verse places the righteous in bliss, the positive side of that division.
The section’s lowest outcome follows the formed human; this next verse says the wicked are in Hell, the opposite of the righteous in 82:13.
The section reserves an enduring reward for believers who do good; this next verse says the one who purifies the soul succeeds, the positive direction named in 91:8.
The section contrasts a low outcome with the faithful exception; this next verse says the one who corrupts the soul fails, opposite the purification and success in 91:9.
The section’s root note names a support that keeps something from falling; this verse contrasts a foundation on piety with one at a crumbling edge that collapses with its builder into the Fire.
The section’s dictionary form قِوَام means what holds a thing up; this verse contrasts the firmly rooted tree with a bad word like a tree uprooted from the earth, having no stability.
The section places the human’s lowest outcome beside an exception; this verse calls disbelievers the worst of created beings, and its next verse supplies the opposite group.
The section’s exception is for those who believe and do good; this next verse calls such people the best of created beings, completing the worst/best contrast begun in 98:6.
The section sets the low outcome against the faithful exception; this passage places the record of the righteous in Illiyyin, a specific counterpart to the wicked record in 83:7.
The section names the low outcome as “lowest of the low”; this next verse makes the nearer-life preference end in Hell, opposite the garden promised to those who fear God in 79:41.
The section’s believers and doers of good receive an uncut reward; this next verse says the Garden is the refuge of the one who feared God’s standing and restrained desire.
The section contrasts a human lowered with believers’ good works; this verse says good words ascend to God and righteous deeds raise them, giving deeds an upward trajectory.
The section names the lowest depth as a fate; this verse promises believers lofty, built chambers above one another, a specific elevated counterpart.
The section contrasts lowering with the reward for steadfast servants; this verse promises them lofty rooms in Paradise for their patience.
The section promises believers who do good a reward that is not cut off; this verse promises such believers secure upper rooms in Paradise and calls that an excellent reward.
The section’s exception turns on belief and righteous works; this verse says wealth and children do not bring nearness, but believers who do good receive multiplied reward and secure lofty chambers.
The section’s body is sent to the lowest; this verse depicts faces humbled and exhausted, the first group in a passage that contrasts their Fire with the elevated garden of 88:10.
The section places lowliness beside an enduring reward; this verse gives the opposing group a “lofty garden,” completing the contrast begun with the humbled faces in 88:2.
The section’s reward is غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, not cut off; this verse contrasts what passes away with what remains with God, clarifying the durability of that reward.
The section lowers a created human and promises believers a lasting reward; this verse says all who are upon the earth perish, the mortal side of that contrast.
The section’s human body is lowered while its reward is uncut; this verse says the Lord of Majesty and Honor remains, the enduring side of the contrast begun in 55:26.
The section promises believers an uncut reward for righteous deeds; this verse calls lasting good works better than worldly wealth and children for reward and hope.
The section’s body has a downward end while believers receive enduring recompense; this verse contrasts worldly provision with what remains with God and is better.
The section’s body is lowered while its faithful exception receives a lasting reward; this verse says people prefer the nearer life, which 87:17 contrasts with the lasting Hereafter.
The section promises a reward not cut off; this next verse says the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life, completing 87:16.
The section sends the human down from a high standing; Pharaoh’s nearby claim “I am your highest lord” is followed by punishment in 79:25, exposing the reversal of self-exaltation.
The section’s high-to-low body is reversed here: believers and the learned are raised in rank, and the command انشزوا tells people to rise when asked.
The section’s low outcome for some is set against its faithful exception; this verse opens the opposing group with faces made glad and ease, before 88:10 locates them in a lofty garden.
The section’s dictionary note says a support keeps a thing standing; this verse speaks of God raising the heavens without visible pillars, an elevated structure whose support is not seen.
The section’s 95:7 asks why people deny after creation and return; this next verse says Pharaoh was shown the signs but denied them, continuing the passage about the earth-cycle in 20:55.
The section distinguishes the faithful from those lowered; this next verse says the bright faces are smiling and rejoicing, continuing the group in 80:38.
The section’s low end is contrasted with a faithful exception; this next verse says darkness covers the dusty faces of 80:40, continuing that group’s outcome.
The section’s downward outcome follows from denial; this next verse identifies the faces in 80:40 and 80:41 as those of disbelievers and sinners.
The section asks what makes people deny judgment; this next verse says the wicked will burn there on the Day of Recompense, specifying when the fate of 82:14 occurs.
The section’s image turns from formed humanity to distinct outcomes; this next verse says the soul is shown its wickedness and its piety, continuing the proportioning in 91:7.
The section’s well-formed human can be lowered; this verse says people who fail to use their hearts, eyes, and ears are like cattle, even further astray.
The section gives earth as the body’s destination; this verse says God revives the earth after its death, a specific parallel to bodies emerging after return to earth.
The section links human creation and return to the ground; this verse describes God reviving dead earth, a land-level counterpart to the body’s return and re-emergence.
The section’s q-w-m root includes standing; this verse names people remembering God while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides as they reflect on creation.
The section’s root note gives the one-time act of rising upright; this command to “stand” (وَقُومُوا) before God uses that bodily sense in prayer.
The section’s q-w-m root includes literal standing; this verse names remembering God while standing, sitting, or lying on one’s sides after prayer.
The section’s root note describes upright standing; this verse pairs standing with prostration in the night worship of the servants of the Merciful.
The section’s q-w-m root names a bodily rising; this command tells the Prophet’s audience to stand for God singly or in pairs and then reflect.
The section’s root note names standing upright; this verse describes a worshipper prostrating and standing while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy.
The section names al-Qayyūm in its dictionary account of resurrection; this verse calls God الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ, the living Sustainer, grounding the human’s support in the One who sustains.
The section’s q-w-m root carries the sense of what stands and sustains; this verse describes God as قائمًا بالقسط, upholding justice, a moral use of that uprightness.
The section’s root note makes uprightness more than bodily form; this verse commands believers to be قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ, standing firmly for justice even against themselves or kin.
The section’s root note joins standing with support; this verse commands believers to be قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ and witnesses in justice, extending uprightness into conduct.
The section’s image of a human held upright meets a moral use of the q-w-m family here: messengers and the Balance are sent so people may uphold justice.
The section’s dictionary form قِوَام means support; this verse uses قَوَّامُونَ for those responsible for maintaining others, a social rather than bodily form of support.
The section divides human outcomes by what people do; this verse says each person will have degrees according to their deeds, linking action with rank at judgment.

The section’s secondary بلد sense pictures a camel placing its chest on the ground; this verse asks people to look at the camel’s creation, focusing on the same animal’s bodily form without depicting its kneeling.
The section’s image turns on upright height and support; this next verse asks how the sky was raised, continuing 88:17’s invitation to observe created forms.
The section’s dictionary form قِوَام names what keeps a thing upright; this next verse asks how mountains were set firm, continuing the created-order scene of 88:17 and 88:18.
The section connects the body to the ground; this next verse asks how the earth was spread out, completing the sequence of created forms in 88:17, 88:18, and 88:19.
The section describes human proportion and an upright form; this verse speaks of the raised sky and the balance set in creation, pairing height with measured order.
The section’s تقويم describes setting things right; this next verse commands that the balance not be transgressed, continuing the raised-sky and balance image of 55:7.
The section’s form is made upright and proportioned; this next verse commands just measure and forbids reducing the balance, completing the measured-order passage.

The section’s secondary dictionary sense for بلد uses an exposed ostrich egg as an image of lowliness; this verse’s بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ are concealed eggs, reversing exposure into protection. The Qur’an does not specify an ostrich.

The section’s secondary dictionary sense for بلد describes a camel lowering its chest to the ground when it kneels; this verse says sacrificial camels fall onto their sides before they are eaten. It is a different kind of falling.
